questions.stem: A note states the Calvin cycle needs 2 ATP and 3 NADPH per CO2; identify the error.

options.text: The ATP and NADPH values are swapped
Both values should be 2
Both values should be 3
NADPH is not used in the cycle

questions.explanation: The correct values are 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, so the note swaps them. Option B and C each fix only one value incorrectly.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Leaf area index and light interception
questions.learningObjective: Compute light intercepted from an LAI curve
questions.stem: If interception follows 1 - exp(-0.5*LAI) and LAI is 2, what fraction is intercepted?
questions.explanation: 1 - exp(-0.5*2) = 1 - exp(-1) = 1 - 0.368 = 0.632. Using the exponential extinction model gives the intercepted fraction.
questions.hint: Compute 1 minus e to the minus one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Ion fluxes that open a stoma
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the H+-ATPase in stomatal opening
questions.stem: The guard-cell H+-ATPase contributes to opening by

options.text: Pumping protons out, hyperpolarising the membrane for K+ uptake
Pumping protons in, depolarising the membrane
Synthesising ATP from proton gradients
Breaking down K+ channels

questions.explanation: The H+-ATPase pumps protons out, hyperpolarising the membrane so K+ channels open. Option B reverses the pump direction.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Stomatal pore area as a fraction of the leaf
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment measuring pore area fraction
questions.stem: Design an experiment to estimate stomatal pore area fraction on a leaf.

answer.exemplar: Take epidermal peels, image under a microscope, count stomata and measure pore dimensions, then compute total pore area divided by image area.

questions.explanation: Microscopy of epidermal peels gives stomatal counts and pore dimensions, from which the area fraction follows. Sampling multiple fields improves accuracy.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compute stomatal density from a micrograph
questions.stem: A micrograph shows 45 stomata in a 0.25 mm2 field; what is the density per mm2?
questions.explanation: Density is 45 divided by 0.25, or 180 stomata per mm2. Dividing count by field area gives density.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the trade-off between cooling and water loss
questions.stem: High stomatal conductance cools a leaf but risks

options.text: Excessive water loss and desiccation
Too much CO2 uptake
Reduced light absorption
Increased photorespiration

questions.explanation: Open stomata cool by transpiration but also lose water, risking desiccation. Option B is wrong because more CO2 uptake is beneficial.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret ABA accumulation data

stimulus.body: A graph plots leaf ABA concentration (ng g-1 FW) versus soil water content (%): 40% 5, 30% 12, 20% 35, 10% 90.

questions.stem: At which soil water content does ABA rise most sharply?

options.text: 40% to 30%, a small increase
30% to 20%, a moderate increase
20% to 10%, the largest increase
No change occurs across the range

questions.explanation: ABA jumps from 35 to 90 between 20% and 10% soil water, the largest increase. Option B captures a smaller rise.

questions.stem: A note says blue light opens stomata by degrading ABA in guard cells; what is wrong?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compute Pfr proportion from red and far-red photon fluxes
questions.stem: If red photon flux is 100 and far-red is 50, and Pfr fraction equals red/(red+far-red), what is it?
questions.explanation: 100 divided by (100 + 50) equals 0.667. Applying the given formula yields the Pfr proportion.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the critical night length
questions.stem: The critical night length in photoperiodism is

options.text: The night length above which a short-day plant flowers
The day length above which any plant flowers
The minimum light intensity for photosynthesis
The temperature at which flowering stops

questions.explanation: The critical night length is the threshold above which short-day plants flower. Option B confuses day length with night length.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment testing vernalisation
questions.stem: Design an experiment to test whether cold exposure is required for flowering in winter wheat.

answer.exemplar: Grow two groups of wheat seedlings, expose one to 4 C for six weeks and keep the other at 20 C, then move both to warm long days and record flowering time.

questions.explanation: A cold-treated group versus a warm control isolates the vernalisation requirement, and flowering time quantifies the effect. Keeping other conditions identical controls confounders.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Photoperiod and flowering in a data set
questions.learningObjective: Explain an exception in flowering data
questions.stem: A short-day plant flowers at 8 h but not at 16 h day length; an exception occurs if a night break is added at 8 h because

options.text: The long night is split, preventing flowering
Extra light always increases flowering
The plant becomes long-day
Temperature rises and inhibits flowering

questions.explanation: A night break splits the long night, so even at 8 h day length the plant may not flower. Option B assumes light always promotes flowering.
questions.hint: A pulse can break the night.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Predict bending when light is removed
questions.stem: If a unilaterally illuminated shoot is suddenly placed in darkness, bending will

options.text: Continue briefly then stop as auxin redistributes evenly
Reverse immediately toward the former light
Accelerate because darkness removes inhibition
Stop instantly with no further growth

questions.explanation: The existing auxin gradient persists briefly, so bending continues then stops as auxin redistributes. Option D ignores the residual gradient.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain negative gravitropism in shoots
questions.stem: A horizontal shoot bends upward because

options.text: Auxin accumulates on the lower side and promotes elongation there
Auxin accumulates on the upper side and inhibits growth
Gravity destroys auxin on the lower side
Shoots lack a gravitropic response

questions.explanation: In shoots, auxin accumulates on the lower side and promotes elongation, bending the shoot upward. Option B reverses the accumulation side.
questions.hint: Shoots grow up, roots grow down.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain apical dominance in terms of source-sink auxin
questions.stem: Why does a strong apical bud suppress the growth of lower lateral buds?

answer.exemplar: The apical bud is a strong auxin source; auxin transported down the stem inhibits lateral bud outgrowth, so removing the apex releases the buds.

questions.explanation: Auxin from the apex suppresses lateral bud growth, maintaining apical dominance. Removing the apex eliminates this inhibition and releases the buds.
